thread.title: I continue to receive messages and comments from Apple ( AAP

author: Bill Maurer
title: I continue to receive messages and comments from Apple ( AAP
text:
I continue to receive messages and comments from Apple ( AAPL ) shareholders that are frustrated with the company's dividend policy. With over $160 billion in net cash at the end of the most recent period , and management likely to repatriate most to all of its foreign funds, investors are wondering if they will get a large dividend raise at some point. Unfortunately, I think that the company should stick to the course it is currently on, which means I don't think expectations should be that high for the dividend moving forward. This thought process, in my opinion, is only strengthened by the recent pullback in Apple shares seen below.
( Source: Yahoo Finance )
Late last week, Apple shares went ex-dividend on the latest quarterly payment of $0.63 per share. This will be the fourth payout at that rate, which implies that the next declaration could be a dividend raise. While some thought Apple could announce major dividend news at the last earnings report thanks to tax cuts, Apple always updates investors at its fiscal Q2 report. That will be in either late April or early May, and I expect that report will see a continuation of dividend raises as we've seen in recent years. The chart below shows Apple's recent dividend history, with the year below representing the new payout announced that year, so for instance last year gets the $0.63 payout that was announced in 2017.
( Source: Apple dividend history page - early dividends adjusted for split)
In 2017, the company announced a six cent per share raise to the dividend, bringing it to $0.63 per quarter. Let's assume that we get a similar raise this year, but I'll give an extra penny to $0.70 to make some math easier. That would be equal to a $2.80 annual payout. While some might argue that this is still not enough, it's a huge increase from the roughly $1.51 shareholders were getting on an adjusted annual basis pre-split when the dividend was reintroduced in 2012.
Now if Apple shares were still near their all-time high of $180.10, I might be singing a different tune. At that price, our hypothetical dividend of $2.80 per year yields 1.555%. But as of Friday's low, the new yield would be 1.864%, a difference of more than 30 basis points. Not only is that a major difference in yield, but that low of $150.24 also allows Apple to repurchase shares in the open market at a much lower level than it did in the most recent period, as seen below. This graphic does not include accelerated repurchase programs, like the one currently scheduled to end this month.
( Source: Apple's latest 10-Q filing, page 16 ) 
Let's think about a buyback in terms of cash, and I'll use $10 billion for that argument. At current rates, Apple is earning about 2.00% annually after taxes on its cash pile, which for that $10 billion equals $200 million in interest income after-tax or about 4 cents per share currently. Buying back those shares would reduce net income by that $200 million, but earnings per share would actually benefit overall due to the lower diluted share count (about 1.31% at current prices times the more than $11 expected this fiscal period ). Since EPS is the more prominently cited metric, investors would likely celebrate this improvement.
However, let's think about the situation in another way. That $10 billion repurchase reduces net income by $200 million, which also would reduce free cash flow by $200 million. At Friday's low, we're talking about 66.56 million shares that could be bought back. At the theoretical $2.80 annual payout we used above, Apple would save almost $186.4 million in the next year on dividend payments. Thus, the company is only losing about $14 million in cash over the next year, because the lower net income is almost completely offset by reduced total dividend payments with a lower share count.
While on the topic of the share count, some investors may not realize the progress Apple has made on this front. In roughly five years, the number of shares outstanding has come down more than 22.8%, as seen in the chart below, and the peak was actually a little higher than my start point. This is a decline of just under 1.5 billion shares, with us about to pass below the 5 billion level very shortly. For this chart, I'm only using the fiscal Q1 10-Q filings, and the dates quoted vary depending on that year's filing.
( Source: Apple quarterly filings ) 
On Friday, Apple shares were just 14 cents away from being $30 off their all-time high, a pullback of almost 16.6%. With that dramatic decline recently, I'm arguing today that the company should stick with the status quo - that's favoring buybacks over dividends. Apple can still increase the dividend at a decent pace moving forward, but I don't see why it should just give money away to investors when it can reduce the share count, improve EPS, help support the stock when it is falling, etc., with more buybacks. While this might be a disappointment for those looking for a massive dividend hike, I think it is a better strategy for the long run, one that will allow for more consistent dividend hikes in the future.
